strengths: Introduces a large, multi-domain, globally distributed benchmark (17 cities, 11 indicators across 6 domains) that fills a real gap between generic urban imagery benchmarks and socioeconomic-sensing tasks, providing a valuable resource for the community.

Evaluates a comprehensive set of 17 state-of-the-art LLVMs (open-source and proprietary, varying scales) under three complementary evaluation paradigms (Direct, Normalized, Feature-Based Regression), enabling multi-angle analysis of model capability.

Careful and transparent dataset construction pipeline: documents indicator selection rationale (perceptual relevance test + Pearson correlation redundancy removal), multiple data sources, and image acquisition details (satellite + street view, different APIs per region).

Provides several useful ablation-style analyses beyond the main leaderboard: impact of satellite imagery, number of street-view images, city-level variation in GDP prediction, and comparison of direct vs normalized estimation preferences per task, which yield actionable insights (e.g., feature-based regression outperforms zero-shot prediction).
Good reproducibility support with detailed prompts (Table 4), example failure cases (model refusals), and appendix listing of all 28 candidate indicators and sources.
Findings are of practical significance for urban planning/SDG-tracking communities and clearly motivate future work (fine-tuning, CoT prompting, agent frameworks).
weaknesses: The three evaluation paradigms are not on equal footing: Feature-Based Regression involves training a supervised LASSO model with 5-fold cross-validation on ground truth, while Direct/Normalized are zero-shot; concluding that LLVMs are better as 'feature enhancers' than 'predictors' conflates the effect of supervised training with the LLVM's inherent capability, which is a significant confound not adequately addressed.

Sample sizes per task are highly uneven and sometimes small (e.g., Life Expectancy n=193, Violent Crime n=389), yet R2 and nRMSE are reported without confidence intervals or significance testing, making cross-task and cross-model comparisons potentially unreliable.

Geographic coverage is heavily skewed: many indicators are restricted to US/UK only, undermining the claimed 'global' and cross-cultural generalization angle that motivates using LLVMs in the first place.

The paper does not compare against non-LLVM baselines (e.g., the classical CV/contrastive-learning methods discussed in related work, like Fan et al. or UrbanCLIP) so it is unclear how much room for improvement or how competitive LLVMs are relative to prior specialized methods rather than only to each other.

Some analyses are based on single examples or small subsets (e.g., street-view image quantity ablation with only one model on one task; satellite-imagery ablation with one model and three tasks), limiting generalizability of the qualitative claims drawn from them.

The explanations for observed phenomena (e.g., why Gemma outperforms Qwen, why larger models sometimes underperform, why certain cities show higher R2) are largely post-hoc narrative without additional controlled experiments or statistical support.

Minor writing/typo issues (e.g., 'leisre-time', inconsistent indicator counts) and some inconsistency between text ('11 indicators') and appendix tables that could confuse readers about exact task counts and coverage.

strengths: The benchmark has broad nominal coverage: 17 cities across multiple continents, 11 indicators across 6 socioeconomic domains, and 17 LLVMs evaluated under 3 distinct evaluation paradigms, which is a reasonable step toward systematizing this application area.
The paper identifies a real gap: prior urban-imagery benchmarks (CityBench, UrBench) are not tailored to socioeconomic indicator prediction, and prior LLVM socioeconomic works are narrower in scope.

Several exploratory analyses (impact of satellite imagery, effect of number of street-view images, city-level variation in GDP prediction) provide some useful, concrete observations that could guide follow-up work.
The paper documents its data sources and prompt templates in reasonable detail, which aids partial reproducibility.
weaknesses: No comparison to classical CV/contrastive-learning baselines (e.g., the CNN-based method of Fan et al. or contrastive urban imagery embeddings) that the paper itself criticizes in the introduction; without this, the claim that LLVMs are more capable across countries/modalities than classical methods is never actually tested, undermining the paper's central motivation.

The indicator selection process (removing 17 of 28 collected indicators via 'perceptual relevance' judgment and pairwise Pearson correlation pruning) is subjective and potentially reduces the benchmark's comprehensiveness and comparability to prior work; the correlation-based removal logic (dropping obesity because it correlates with mental health) is questionable, since correlated indicators can still carry distinct, useful signal.

The Feature-Based Regression paradigm is not really evaluating the LLVM's own prediction ability in a zero-shot sense — it trains a supervised LASSO regressor on LLVM-derived features with 5-fold CV, which conflates the contribution of the (trained, data-fitted) regressor with that of the vision-language model; no baseline is given for regression on simple, non-LLVM image features (e.g., off-the-shelf CNN embeddings) to isolate whether the reported gains actually stem from the LLVM's feature extraction versus the regression step itself.

A critical and unaddressed confound is memorization/data leakage: for well-known cities and coarse indicators (e.g., 'Beijing/Shanghai GDP', 'Mumbai vs Moscow economic level'), LLMs likely already encode approximate values from pretraining text corpora rather than inferring them from the accompanying images; the paper never disentangles genuine visual grounding from prior world knowledge (e.g., via a no-image but city-name-only ablation across more tasks/models), which is essential for a benchmark claiming to test 'visual socioeconomic sensing.'

Most quantitative explanations in the results/discussion sections are speculative post-hoc narratives ('may be attributed to...', 'one possible explanation is...') without additional evidence, statistical tests, or ablations to support them, reducing the scientific rigor of the analysis.

Sample sizes are inconsistent and sometimes very small across tasks/cities (e.g., Life Expectancy: 193 satellite images; Violent Crime: 389), and the arbitrary sampling caps (500 for country-specific, 1000 for global indicators) are not justified nor accounted for in reported variance, raising concerns about statistical reliability of cross-task comparisons.

Key ablations are extremely narrow: the satellite-imagery-impact study uses only one model (Gemini-2.0-Flash) and 3 tasks, and the street-view-image-quantity study uses only one model (Llama4-Maverick) and 1 task, which is insufficient to support the generalized claims made in the discussion.

The differentiation from very closely related concurrent work (e.g., [24] 'What can LLM tell us about cities?', which also evaluates LLMs on socioeconomic tasks across granularities with multiple paradigms) is not rigorously established beyond scale, leaving the novelty claim ('first benchmark to systematically evaluate...') somewhat overstated.

No human-performance baseline or theoretical upper bound is provided to contextualize how much of the observed low R2 is due to inherent task difficulty (weak visual-indicator correlation) versus model limitations.

Minor issues: numerous typos/informal language (e.g., 'leisre-time'), inconsistent notation, and some claims in the abstract/intro (e.g., 'first benchmark') are not sufficiently substantiated by the related work discussion.

strengths: Introduces a large, well-organized multi-modal benchmark (CityLens) covering 17 cities across 6 continents, 11 indicators in 6 socioeconomic domains, combining satellite and street view imagery -- filling a genuine gap since prior urban-LLVM benchmarks (CityBench, UrBench) do not focus specifically on socioeconomic sensing.

Evaluates a broad and current set of 17 LLVMs (open-source and proprietary, various scales) under three distinct and well-motivated evaluation paradigms (Direct Metric Prediction, Normalized Estimation, Feature-Based Regression), enabling a more complete picture of model capability than a single-task/single-metric study.

Provides useful supplementary analyses beyond the main results table: impact of satellite imagery, effect of street-view image count, city-level performance variation, and preference for direct vs. normalized estimation per task -- these add practical insight for future benchmark/method design.
Careful documentation of data sources, indicator selection rationale (perceptual relevance + Pearson correlation de-duplication), and prompt templates (Appendix), which supports reproducibility.

The observation that feature-based regression (LLVM as feature extractor + LASSO) outperforms zero-shot direct/normalized prediction is a reasonably interesting empirical finding with actionable implications (e.g., fine-tuning direction, CoT prompting) for the community.
weaknesses: No comparison to non-LLVM baselines (e.g., the classical CV/contrastive-learning methods discussed at length in Related Work, such as Fan et al. [14] or knowledge-graph methods) despite the paper's framing that LLVMs should overcome classical methods' limitations; without such baselines it is unclear whether LLVM-based approaches are actually competitive or merely 'not terrible'.

Absolute performance is low across almost all tasks/models (mean R2 often 0.2-0.35, sometimes near zero or negative), which raises questions about the practical significance and actionable value of the benchmark's findings beyond 'LLVMs are still bad at this' -- a somewhat expected conclusion.

The Feature-Based Regression paradigm is not a fair apples-to-apples comparison with the two zero-shot predictor paradigms, since it involves training a supervised LASSO regressor with 5-fold cross-validation on the LLVM-derived features; the paper's conclusion that this paradigm 'significantly outperforms' the others should be qualified given this asymmetry.

City/indicator coverage is uneven and misleading as 'global': many indicators (transport, crime, mental health, bachelor ratio) are restricted to only 3 US or 3 UK cities, while the 17-city, 6-continent framing is only true for a handful of indicators (GDP, population, building height, accessibility to health).

No discussion of potential data leakage/memorization -- LLMs may have memorized well-known city-level statistics (e.g., GDP, population) from pretraining text corpora rather than deriving them from the provided imagery, which could confound interpretation of 'visual reasoning' capability, especially in the Direct/Normalized paradigms.

Sampling for global tasks (30 random geographic points per city, ~10 street-view images each) is relatively sparse and could introduce substantial noise into per-city comparisons (e.g., Section 3.4.1's city-level analysis), yet no uncertainty quantification (confidence intervals, variance across resamples) is reported for any of the reported R2/nRMSE values.

Several explanations for observed patterns (e.g., why Gemma3-4B outperforms Qwen2.5VL-3B, why Shanghai/San Francisco perform better than Mumbai/Moscow) are speculative post-hoc narratives without further empirical verification (e.g., no controlled ablation isolating 'urban design homogeneity' or 'architecture/training process' as causal factors).

The paper lacks a human-performance baseline or expert-derived upper bound, making it hard to judge how much of the low performance is due to model limitations versus inherent task difficulty/ceiling effects from a purely visual signal.

strengths: Large-scale, comprehensive benchmark construction spanning 17 cities, 11 socioeconomic indicators across 6 domains, with both satellite and street view imagery, representing significant data engineering effort.

Evaluation of 17 diverse LVLMs (open-source and proprietary) across three distinct evaluation paradigms (Direct Metric Prediction, Normalized Estimation, Feature-Based Regression) provides a thorough comparative picture of current model capabilities.

Rich set of ancillary analyses: city-level variation, modality ablation (street view vs satellite), image quantity effects, CoT vs standard prompting, reasoning model comparisons, vision encoder comparisons, and fine-tuning experiments, which together provide useful diagnostic insight into why models fail.

Strong reproducibility and ethics considerations: an open-source Mapillary-based variant of the dataset is provided, alongside detailed data source documentation, misuse disclaimers, and a preliminary bias audit across Global North/South cities.
Error case analysis and a qualitative hypothesis about low-level vs high-level visual reasoning in LVLMs adds interpretive depth beyond pure benchmark numbers.
The paper acknowledges its own methodological choices (e.g., rejecting multiple-choice formats, discussing image count trade-offs) with reasonable justification grounded in related literature.
weaknesses: Overall predictive performance is weak across nearly all tasks and models (R2 often near zero or negative), raising the question of how much genuine scientific insight the benchmark yields beyond 'LVLMs are not good at this yet'; the practical utility of the benchmark as a diagnostic tool is not clearly established.

The baselines used for comparison (UrbanCLIP, UrbanVLP) are limited; no comparison to more recent domain-specific socioeconomic prediction methods (e.g., contrastive learning models mentioned in intro like MuseCL, Yong & Zhou 2024) is included in the main benchmark table, despite being discussed in related work.

Indicator selection process (Pearson correlation filtering, perceptual relevance human test) is described briefly without rigorous methodology or inter-rater reliability details, making the selection process somewhat subjective and hard to reproduce exactly.

Sample sizes for several tasks are quite small (e.g., Life Expectancy n=193, Violent Crime n=389), which may limit statistical robustness of R2 estimates, especially when comparing 17 models across many task-model combinations without confidence intervals or significance testing.

The fine-tuning experiment (Table 2) is presented as an 'upper bound' demonstration but is fairly preliminary (three models, limited tasks, no details on fine-tuning data size/held-out splits relative to test regions), and could suffer from data leakage concerns between fine-tuning data and benchmark regions since both are drawn from 'additional CityLens data.'

Geographic coverage, while broad, is heavily skewed toward US/UK for many indicators due to data availability, undermining the claimed 'global' scope for several key tasks (e.g., transport, crime, education tasks are US-only).

The interpretive narrative sections (e.g., hypotheses about low-level vs high-level visual concepts, explanations for why Gemma outperforms Qwen) are largely speculative post-hoc explanations without controlled experiments to verify these causal claims.

Given the acceptance rate context, the novelty is primarily in benchmark scale/scope rather than methodological innovation; the three evaluation paradigms build directly on existing techniques (GeoLLM-style normalization, Fan et al. visual taxonomy) with limited technical novelty of their own.

strengths: Large nominal scope: 17 cities, 11 indicators across 6 domains, 17 LVLMs, and 3 evaluation paradigms, representing a substantial data-collection and engineering effort.

Diverse set of supplementary analyses (modality ablation, image-count ablation, CoT vs standard prompting, vision-encoder comparison, fine-tuning, Mapillary open-source variant) that probe multiple angles of LVLM behavior.
Reasonable attention to reproducibility (public pano-id lists, open Mapillary alternative) and to ethics (privacy, geographic bias, misuse declaimer).

Some individually interesting empirical observations (e.g., street-view-only often matches or beats street+satellite; task-dependent preference between direct vs normalized prediction; inconsistent effect of CoT across models/tasks).
weaknesses: Overall predictive performance is very low or near-zero/negative across most tasks and settings, which makes it hard to tell whether this reflects genuine LVLM limitations or noisy/mismatched ground-truth labels (e.g., 1km-resolution global rasters averaged over an arbitrary satellite-image footprint, ZIP-to-census-tract crosswalks, random 30-point sampling per satellite tile) — the benchmark's label construction itself introduces substantial uncertainty that is never quantified or bounded (no noise floor, no human/oracle baseline for comparison).

Heterogeneous evaluation units (census tract, MSOA, satellite-image footprint) and heterogeneous street-view sources (Google vs Baidu vs Mapillary) are mixed within and across tasks, undermining the validity of cross-task and cross-city comparisons that the paper nonetheless makes (e.g., the city-level GDP comparison, the Global North/South bias audit).

Many of the explanatory narratives throughout Section 3 (e.g., why Shanghai/Sao Paulo perform well, why CoT helps House Price but hurts Drive Ratio, why Gemma outperforms Qwen) are purely speculative post-hoc storytelling without any controlled test, ablation, or statistical support — this weakens the scientific contribution to mostly anecdotal commentary.

The Feature-Based Regression paradigm, which produces the strongest and most-reported results, actually evaluates a classical LASSO regressor trained on LVLM-derived scalar scores rather than the LVLM's own predictive ability; this conflates 'LVLM as feature extractor + supervised regressor' with 'LVLM socioeconomic reasoning,' making the headline comparisons to baselines like UrbanVLP somewhat apples-to-oranges.

Sample sizes are small and inconsistent across tasks (e.g., Life Expectancy n=193, Violent Crime n=389), and the paper does not report confidence intervals or variance over repeated runs, so differences between models (e.g., 4.3%/6.8% 'relative drops' between Gemma3-12B and 27B) are likely within noise.

The fine-tuning experiment (Table 2), used to claim a 'preliminary upper bound' and to motivate the entire benchmark's significance, is described in only a few sentences with no detail on training data size, split, hyperparameters, or whether train/test leakage was controlled — this is too thin to support the strong claims made from it.

The normalized (0.0–9.9) estimation protocol coarsely quantizes continuous indicators, and no analysis is given of how much of the 'low performance' is attributable to this coarse binning versus genuine model failure.

No human-expert or trivial-baseline (e.g., city-average predictor) reference point is reported for most settings, making it difficult to assess whether reported R2/nRMSE values represent meaningful model understanding versus chance-level or mean-reverting behavior (the paper itself notes 'predictions collapse toward city-wide averages' but doesn't quantify this against a mean-predictor baseline).

Model coverage and settings are inconsistent across experiments (different subsets of models/tasks tested in different ablations), making it hard to build a coherent overall picture or to reproduce specific claimed comparisons.
The appendix 'hypothesis' on low-level vs high-level visual concepts (A.10) is purely speculative and unfalsifiable, reading more as padding than as a rigorous contribution.

strengths: Introduces the most comprehensive benchmark to date for evaluating LVLMs on urban socioeconomic sensing, spanning 17 cities, 11 indicators across 6 domains, and 17 models, which fills a clear gap in the literature.

Employs three complementary evaluation paradigms (Direct Metric Prediction, Normalized Estimation, Feature-Based Regression), enabling nuanced analysis of different ways LVLMs can be used for this task.

Extensive supplementary experiments (modality ablation, image quantity scaling, CoT vs standard prompting, reasoning-model comparison, vision-encoder ablation, nonlinear regressors, caption-embedding approach, multiple-choice format exploration) provide a thorough diagnostic picture rather than a single headline result.
Fine-tuning experiments (Table 2) offer a useful upper-bound estimate showing the potential of domain-adapted LVLMs, strengthening the paper's motivation.
Strong reproducibility efforts: an open-source Mapillary-based dataset variant is provided alongside the Google/Baidu version, along with pano-id lists, download scripts, and code.
Thoughtful ethics statement and a preliminary geographic bias audit (Global North vs. Global South performance gap) that responsibly surfaces fairness concerns rather than glossing over them.
Interesting counter-intuitive findings (e.g., street view alone rivaling street view + satellite, non-monotonic scaling with model size) that could inform future work on multimodal urban sensing.
weaknesses: Many tasks rely on small sample sizes (e.g., 193 regions for Life Expectancy, 389 for Violent Crime), which limits the statistical reliability of reported R² values and cross-model comparisons for these tasks.

Geographic coverage is uneven and often reduces to US/UK-only for many indicators (transport, crime, several health indicators, education), which somewhat undercuts the claimed 'global' and '17-city' scope for those specific tasks.

Most Direct/Normalized Estimation results hover around zero or negative R², so the main empirical takeaway is largely that current LVLMs fail at this task in a zero-shot setting — a result that is plausible a priori and provides comparatively less novel scientific insight beyond confirming difficulty.

The Feature-Based Regression paradigm evaluates LVLMs as feature extractors feeding a separately trained LASSO/nonlinear regressor, which conflates the LVLM's zero-shot capability with the regressor's fitting power and makes direct comparison with end-to-end trained baselines (e.g., UrbanVLP) somewhat apples-to-oranges.

Several causal explanations offered in the analysis (e.g., why Gemma outperforms Qwen, why certain cities perform better) are post-hoc and speculative, without controlled experiments isolating the proposed factors.

No human-performance baseline is reported for the actual prediction tasks (only a qualitative feasibility check during indicator selection), making it hard to contextualize how far LVLM performance is from an achievable upper bound using the same visual inputs.
Single-run evaluations without reporting variance/temperature settings raise concerns about the stability of point estimates given the stochastic nature of LLM/LVLM outputs.

The 13 visual features used in Feature-Based Regression are inherited from prior work (Fan et al., 2023) without validation that this fixed feature set is sufficient or optimal for the broader set of 11 indicators considered here.
